About: Spherical Mirrors — Walking the Object In

Source

Topic
Reflection at spherical mirrors (Class 12 — Ray Optics)
Simulation
Interactive ray-diagram construction for a spherical mirror
Concept
Walking the object toward the focus of a concave mirror sends the image to infinity — then it reappears virtual, upright and magnified behind the mirror.
Serves
Mirror equation 1/u + 1/v = 1/f, magnification m = −v/u, focal length f = R/2, real vs virtual image behaviour, concave vs convex distinction.
Inquiry
As the object slides from far away toward F, does the real image shrink, grow, or vanish?
Misconception
“A concave mirror always magnifies” / “the image is always behind the mirror.”

Guided Inquiry

1 · Look at the scene

A concave mirror sits on the right. An object (purple arrow) stands on the axis well beyond C (the centre of curvature). Two construction rays are drawn — one parallel to the axis reflecting through F, one through F reflecting parallel. They cross at the image (green arrow).

Notice: the image is real, inverted, and smaller than the object. That is the whole starting picture.

2 · Predict

You will now slide the object toward F. What happens to the image before it reaches F?

3 · Inside C

The object now sits at u = 14 cm, between C and F. The image has moved out past C — still real and inverted, but now taller than the object: m = −2.50.

Walk the slider down and the rest follows: u = 20 cm (= C) gives life-size, m = −1; u = 15 cm gives m = −2; at u = 10 cm (= F) the reflected rays leave parallel and never meet — no image, v = ∞.

4 · Past the focus

The object is now at u = 6 cm, inside F. The two reflected rays leave the mirror diverging, so they can never cross in front of it. Follow them backwards instead — the dashed lines — and they meet behind the mirror.

That intersection is the image: virtual (no light is really there), upright, and magnified, m = +2.50. It is the shaving-mirror regime, and it is the only one a concave mirror has on this side of F.

5 · The convex mirror

The mirror is now convex, object at u = 25 cm. F and C have moved behind it (drawn dashed), so f = −R/2.

Sweep u across its whole range: the image never crosses the mirror, never inverts, never magnifies — virtual, upright, diminished at every distance. A concave mirror runs through the whole zoo; a convex mirror does one thing only, which is why passenger-side mirrors carry “objects are closer than they appear.”

Which sign convention? On this bench every distance is measured from the pole P and counted positive in front of the mirror — so u > 0 always, v > 0 means a real image, and f = R/2 > 0 means concave. NCERT's Cartesian convention measures the same distances along the incident light, which simply flips the sign of u, v and f — that is the row above. Both conventions give the same 1/u + 1/v = 1/f, the same m = −v/u, and the same image.

Mirror equation — real-is-positive convention: u > 0 for a real object; v > 0 for a real image (in front); f = R/2, positive for concave, negative for convex.
Magnification. m < 0 ⇒ inverted (always real for a single mirror); m > 0 ⇒ upright (virtual). |m| > 1 ⇒ enlarged.
At the focal point the reflected rays leave parallel — v is undefined (formally infinite), so the mirror forms no image.
Concave mirror image regimes as u decreases from ∞.

01

At a glance

A spherical mirror stands at the right of a bench, with an object on the principal axis in front of it. You set how far the object is from the mirror, how curved the mirror is, and whether it is concave or convex.

What you'll learn

  • How two construction rays locate the image of an object.
  • How the object distance u, the image distance v and the focal length f are linked.
  • How the position, size and orientation of the image change as the object moves.
  • How a convex mirror differs from a concave one.
The bench as drawn, without the rays. The pole P is the middle of the mirror's surface.

What's on screen

  • Purple arrow: the object. Drag it along the axis.
  • Green arrow: the image. A dashed arrow means a virtual image.
  • Amber ray and cyan ray: the two construction rays.
  • Image panel: v, m, the nature of the image and f.
See itLook at the bench with the opening values. Watch for: the purple object, the green image, and the amber and cyan rays.

03

Two construction rays locate the image

Every point of the object sends out many rays, but two are easy to follow. The image of the arrow's tip is where the reflected rays meet.

  • Ray 1 comes in parallel to the axis and reflects through F.
  • Ray 2 comes in through F and reflects parallel to the axis.
The two rays for the opening values. The reflected rays cross at the image tip.

When the reflected rays spread apart and never cross in front of the mirror, trace them backwards. The sim draws these extensions dashed, and the image sits where they meet behind the mirror.

See itFollow the amber and cyan rays at the opening values. Watch for: both reflected rays crossing at the green image, 15.0 cm from the pole.
04

The mirror equation links u, v and f

Distances are measured from the pole and counted positive in front of the mirror. Then

1/u + 1/v = 1/f,   f = R/2,   m = −v/u
f is positive for a concave mirror and negative for a convex one.
  • A positive v is a real image in front of the mirror. A negative v is a virtual image behind it.
  • A negative m means inverted, and |m| above 1 means enlarged.
  • The Cartesian convention in NCERT measures along the incident light, so u, v and f all change sign. The sim shows both.
u (cm)4530201512
v (cm)12.8615.0020.0030.0060.00
m−0.29−0.50−1.00−2.00−5.00

For concave R = 20 cm, so f = 10 cm.

See itSet u to 15 cm with R = 20 cm. Watch for: v = 30.0 cm and m = −2.00, with the NCERT row reading u −15.0, v −30.0, f −10.0.
05

As the object nears F, the image runs far away

For a concave mirror, 1/v = 1/f − 1/u. As u falls towards f, the right side shrinks towards zero, so v grows without limit and the image grows with it, since m = −v/u.

u (cm)14121110.510
v (cm)3560110210∞
m−2.5−5−10−20∞
  • At u = f the reflected rays leave parallel. They never meet, and no image forms.
  • The sim then draws the ray through C in place of ray 2, because the object sits on F.
  • The image can run past the edge of the bench. Its label then says which way it went.
See itWalk u down from 14 cm to 10 cm with R = 20 cm. Watch for: v climbing from 35 cm, then "no image (rays parallel)" at u = 10.0 cm.
06

Inside F the image is virtual, upright and enlarged

Once u is less than f, the equation gives a negative v. The reflected rays now spread apart, so they cannot cross in front of the mirror. Traced backwards, they meet behind it.

  • At u = 6 cm with f = 10 cm, v = −15 cm and m = +2.5.
  • The image is virtual: no light actually reaches it. It is upright, because m is positive, and 2.5 times as tall as the object.
  • Closer to F the image is larger still. At u = 9 cm, v = −90 cm and m = +10.
  • This is the regime of a shaving mirror: hold it close, inside F, and the face looks enlarged and upright.

A concave mirror therefore runs through every kind of image. Beyond F the image is real and inverted, and inside F it is virtual and upright.

See itWalk u down from 12 cm to 6 cm, through F. Watch for: the image jumping behind the mirror at 6 cm, dashed, with v = −15.0 cm and m = 2.50.
07

A convex mirror gives only small, upright, virtual images

For a convex mirror f = −R/2, so F and C lie behind the mirror, drawn dashed. The equation then gives a negative v for every real object.

  • At u = 25 cm with R = 20 cm, f = −10 cm, v = −7.14 cm and m = +0.29.
  • Here m = |f| / (|f| + u), which is always between 0 and 1.
  • With R = 20 cm, m runs from 0.77 at u = 3 cm down to 0.18 at u = 45 cm.
  • So the image is virtual, upright and diminished at every distance.

A smaller image takes in a wider view, which is why a passenger-side mirror is convex. The small image can make a car look farther away than it is, hence the warning that objects in the mirror are closer than they appear.

See itSwitch to a convex mirror and walk u from 45 cm to 3 cm. Watch for: v staying negative and m staying between 0.18 and 0.77.
08

Where it matters

  • Shaving and make-up mirrors. A concave mirror held inside F gives an upright, enlarged image.
  • Torches and headlamps. A lamp placed at F sends its light out as a parallel beam. This is ray 2 in reverse.
  • Telescope mirrors. Light from a distant star arrives parallel to the axis, so a concave mirror brings it to a focus at F, where v = f.
  • Passenger-side and shop mirrors. Convex mirrors give a wide field of view with a diminished image.
Go deeper: why the drawn rays turn at a flat line

The sim draws each ray turning at the vertical line through the pole, not on the curved surface. This is the paraxial approximation, which is valid for rays close to the axis. Rays far from the axis do not all pass through the same F on a spherical mirror, an effect called spherical aberration. A parabolic mirror removes it.

09

Summary

In one line. A spherical mirror forms an image whose place, size and orientation depend on the object's distance and on the mirror's focal length.

Key points

  • The image is where two reflected construction rays meet, or appear to meet.
  • 1/u + 1/v = 1/f with f = R/2, and m = −v/u.
  • For a concave mirror, u greater than f gives a real, inverted image, and u less than f gives a virtual, upright, enlarged one.
  • A convex mirror always gives a virtual, upright, diminished image.

Common mix-ups

  • "A concave mirror always inverts the image." Inside F it gives an upright one.
  • "An object at F gives an image at F." It gives no image, because the reflected rays are parallel.
  • "A convex mirror can enlarge if the object is close enough." Its |m| stays below 1 at every distance.

Things to try on your own

  • Find the u that gives m = −1 when R = 30 cm.
  • With R = 20 cm, find the u that puts the real image at v = 60 cm.
  • With a convex mirror and R = 10 cm, find the largest |m| you can reach.
